This study investigates why conventional neural networks frequently struggle to solve the high-dimensional Schrödinger equation. By examining the generalization performance from two-layer neural networks, we find that it is due to a well-known optimization issue in machine learning. A specific example illustrates that even though a network achieves low training error, it may not generalize well. We analyze the reasons behind generalization in the high-dimensional Schrödinger context and propose an alternative approach using a Gaussian prior to overcome the non-convex optimization problem and improve generalization. Our proposed method can be used as a starting point for more advanced methods to solve the Schrödinger equation. Numerical results confirm the effectiveness of our proposed method, and it can be combined with other advanced methods to further improve their performance.

In the field of neuroscience, regression models, specifically machine learning techniques, are increasingly being used to analyze neural activity and understand its underlying mechanisms. This work utilizes a temporal series regression approach with Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to model and compare different architectures for simulating neural activity similar to that found in the Caenorhabditis elegans worm. By leveraging advanced deep learning software written in Keras, optimized for high-performance computing on GPU platforms like NVIDIA and AMD, this study marks a significant breakthrough in applying machine learning to neuroscience through efficient, open-source solutions.

For a given stationary vertex configuration of a n-body problem, we identify conditions under which it can be achieved with figures consisting of multiple connected components, which are essentially complex geometric shapes with multiple boundaries. Specifically, we focus on configurations where all particles occupy separate regions in one-dimensional or two-dimensional space. In the one-dimensional case, our condition is straightforward and easily satisfied, but in the two-dimensional scenario, it becomes more complex and involves specific non-degenerate polynomial coefficients. Fortunately, our main constraint only restricts the shape of the individual regions, but it does not impose specific geometric constraints on the overall shape of the space. Interestingly, our findings also include specific theorems that continue to apply even when the space is divided into the simplest possible regions - one-dimensional or two-dimensional spaces divided into one piece each.

A Gelfand pair for a group corresponds to a probability measure on the group that is invariant under left or right action with respect to a subgroup. 
In particular, Gelfand pairs and their associated measures possess certain invariance properties, making them amenable to characterization. 
Notably, a robust Gelfand pair is defined as one that remains Gelfand in every quotient resulting from the removal of any finite set of elements. 
We present a classification of robust Gelfand pairs for the group SL(2,p). 
Additionally, related characterizations for the group SP(2,p) are also provided. 
Lastly, a robust Gelfand pair for p > 2 exists, whereas no such pair exists when p = 2.

This research delves into the molecular pentaquarks, focusing specifically on the $P_{cc}^S$ state with a single strangeness particle and no other, and investigates its possible isoscalar and isovector states. We model its interactions using the Klein-Gordon Regge theory, and derive an effective interaction Lagrangian, ultimately discovering how it couples to the $\gamma$ and $\phi$ mesons. We then develop a comprehensive description of the molecular pentaquarks' properties, including their electromagnetic properties and mass spectra. We further make predictions regarding their observability in experiments, such as PANDA at the FAIR and the BESIII at Beijing.

This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a field has a dimension that is 2 or 3, implying that such algebras are solvable. Additionally, some properties of polynomial identities in these algebras are also explored.

This paper examines the third and fourth order terms in the asymptotic expansion of the wave operator for a cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation on $\mathbb{R}^3$ with a quadratic potential. We achieve this for a restricted class of potentials that are localized and have limited growth. We obtain this result using a novel method based on the Sobolev inequality for Radon transforms, combined with the use of splitting operators in energy spaces and a stable manifolds approach, allowing us to study the behavior of solutions in supercritical Sobolev spaces.

This paper outlines a model of a migration-tonnage process, where the flow of migrants and goods are interdependent. We establish that a migration-tonnage process is a generalized version of a Brownian motion with possibly zero probability and show that it has a unique adaptation. We also establish the continuous and local martingale properties of this adaptation. Furthermore, we discovered that a specific type of migration-tonnage process, which incorporates trade volume, has unique characteristics and can be broken down into its individual components. Finally, we demonstrated the applicability of Ito's formula for this type of process and verified the continuous and local martingale properties of trade volume.

To understand why a star's stars dim, it's crucial to identify any orbital patterns influencing its brightness changes. We studied the star K2-138 using data from the TESS space telescope, analyzing its unique light patterns to confirm the presence of multiple planets. We calculated an accurate timeline for when each planet orbits its star, starting from a close-to-balanced planetary order. We found that the timeline is as follows: starting from a relatively uniform planetary order, we calculated an accurate timeline for when each planet orbits its star. We discovered a sequence of orbital periods for the planets, confirmed through TESS data. We verified the presence of six planets with specific orbital periods, initially hypothesized based on earlier data. We validated our model's accuracy, ensuring it effectively captures the planets' influence on dimming patterns. We found that the timeline for when each planet orbits its star is as follows: starting from a relatively uniform planetary order, we calculated an accurate timeline for when each planet orbits its star. We confirmed the presence of six planets with specific orbital periods, initially hypothesized based on earlier data. We validated our model's accuracy, ensuring it effectively captures the planets' influence on dimming patterns.

We introduce a novel functor, denoted as $\mathfrak{w}_{\mathbf{v}}$, referred to as the authentic Whittaker functor, and we prove that it is a quotient of the endomorphism algebra of the tensor product of two modules, specifically $\mathbb{C}[\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb{C}) \ltimes \mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb{C})]^{\mathbb{C}_q}$ generated by the quantum affine algebra $\mathbb{C}_q[\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb{C})^{\mathbf{v}}]$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the functor $\mathfrak{w}_{\mathbf{v}}$ is equivalent to a module algebra under the action of the Drinfeld--Jimbo quantum affine algebra $\mathbb{C}_q[\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb{C})^{\mathbf{v}}$. Additionally, we establish a quantum affine Schur--Weyl duality by showing that $\mathbb{C}_q[\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb{C})^{\mathbf{v}}]$ acts faithfully on the module category of the authentic Whittaker functor $\mathfrak{w}_{\mathbf{v}}$, and we also prove that the module category is equivalent to the category of the faithful Gelfand

The SiD experiment proposal outlines a particle detector with cutting-edge silicon sensors and diamond-based detection systems for charged particles, utilizing thin silicon sensor blades in a strong magnetic field and nano-structured diamond detectors for precise particle identification. In the original SiD design, highly advanced silicon sensor technology is integrated to minimize particle detection losses, with thin silicon blades in a strong magnetic field and specialized diamond detectors for detailed particle analysis. Although the SiD experiment's basic framework remains, the silicon technology is advancing rapidly, allowing for relaxation of certain design constraints without altering the experiment's fundamental approach. In this paper, we examine how the anticipated advancements in silicon technology can be incorporated into the SiD experiment, with a focus on incorporating triple-gated silicon sensor concepts and advanced silicon physics capabilities. In addition, the global status of silicon technology development and future projections are presented, along with a discussion of how these advancements can be incorporated into the SiD experiment, resulting in reduced particle detection losses.

To investigate the possibility of finding ice VI-like regions in amorphous ices, we conducted molecular dynamics simulations of carbon dioxide and water molecules in hexagonal clusters. Our studies showed that the CO2 cluster exhibits a hexagonal structure similar to that of ice VI, while the water cluster does not. Raising the temperature in the water simulation caused the hexagonal arrangement to transform into a tetrahedral structure, reminiscent of ice Ic. In contrast, the CO2 cluster remained hexagonal up to 600 K. These results suggest that the hexagonal arrangement in the molecular clusters is stable over a wide temperature range, from 100 to 600 K.

This study employs atomic-resolution imaging via Scanning Tunneling Microscopy to examine the surfaces of graphite, gold, and silicon. Utilizing local density of states mapping, the experiment successfully distinguishes between different atomic orbitals on graphite and gold samples, providing clear evidence of these materials' local density of states. Additionally, the results indicate that sodium can be effectively removed from sodium-coated tips, thus enhancing the Scanning Tunneling Microscopy's resolution and reliability.

This paper introduces a pioneering approach to theorems involving domain restrictions in a partial order framework. We establish a method for proving domain restrictions in a partial order, and demonstrate its effectiveness in handling theorems within the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs. We present a novel method for this domain, and compare it to existing approaches. Additionally, we provide a method for proving the equivalence of partial order definitions based on well-known concepts in computer science.

Space weather researchers seek to develop tools that can anticipate and predict Earth's space environment, allowing for timely warnings about potential impacts on satellites. To achieve this, they aim to create accurate forecasts of magnetospheric ULF wave activity, which may pose a threat to operations. Building on existing research showing animals can detect these waves, scientists are working on projects to make the waves audible to humans and animals alike, enabling them to perceive and study the magnetosphere. To bring this goal within reach, researchers are investigating the underlying physics of wave perception and developing a framework for testing wave detection methods. By comparing human and animal hearing ranges to solar wind and magnetic field frequency scales, they can now identify key components necessary for wave perception and devise experiments to demonstrate its feasibility. Ultimately, by making the magnetospheric environment audible, scientists can advance our understanding of the space environment and facilitate communication about potential hazards to satellites in orbit.

A rotating dilaton black string with a specific charge, derived from a logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics model, is extended to a dilaton black membrane for arbitrary rotation. We investigate the thermodynamic properties of these rotating dilaton black membranes by first using the Smarr-Immirzi relation to define mass in terms of the horizon area and determine the temperature and charging capacity. Next, we introduce a Legendre transformation to confirm that the first law and Clausius relation of thermodynamics are satisfied. Furthermore, we calculate the Euclidean action of the dilaton black membrane, and through the variational principle, we find that the charging capacity is properly conjugated to the angular velocity, while the system's phase transitions into a rotating dilaton black string or an extremal rotating dilaton black string, depending on the charging capacity and specific charge, are also explored.

Cognitive architectures are designed to address multiple intelligent behaviors through a single unified system. Melo et al. proposed a declarative memory module in 2018 to enhance cognitive architecture representation capabilities. This paper takes as its starting point the aforementioned work by Melo et al. and presents an innovative recall-based approach as an alternative method for the representation of textual information. The traditional method relies on encoding to generate representations, whereas our novel method leverages a recall-based strategy to extract meaning from text via a conceptualization process grounded in semantic memory. The theoretical framework is accompanied by a simulated example demonstrating its applicability in a cognitive architecture system.

We present a unified approach to generate CCR and CAR algebras through the interplay of creation and annihilation operators in relation to a specific unilateral shift on a Hilbert space, thereby providing an alternative representation of these algebras using a linear transformation on a specific type of C*-algebra, namely Cuntz-Toeplitz C*-algebras. This unified framework gives rise to novel observations and offers a distinct perspective on linking the commutative nature of CCR and CAR algebras, thereby highlighting the essential role of the commutator in their construction.

This paper introduces a minor-step operational semantics for GP 2, a type 2 tagged grammar that generates partial functions. Building on existing research by Lehi\'n and Bonsangue, the proposed semantics expands on their work by providing a step-indexed semantics and addressing previously overlooked aspects of the grammar. In addition, the study includes an in-depth examination of the relationship between GP 2 and the SCD partial correctness compiler, highlighting that GP 2's step semantics aligns with the SCD's step semantics for well-tailored programs.

A new study investigates the effects of photoevaporation and magnetized gas outflows from the TW Hydrae disk using radio observations. By analyzing NOEMA's 120 GHz spectrum, the researchers found no evidence of high-ionized gas in the disk. They used a new model to compare observed emission to disk emission, and this comparison led to the identification of two possible scenarios. In the first scenario, the Meudon3 model with photoevaporation matches the observed emission, but does not account for the central emission. In the second scenario, the Meudon3 model with magnetized outflows fits the observed emission, but does not match pre-existing optical and UV data. These results suggest that TW Hydrae's gas outflow could explain the observed photoevaporation rate, but not the gas emission observed in the UV spectrum.

We establish a factorization of the polynomial variants $\cos(\frac{2\pi}{d})$ with minimal equations in $d$. This leads to an explicit factorization of the polynomial variants of Chebyshev polynomials $T_d(x)$ for all $d$. We also provide a connection to the polynomial variants of Euler's totient function. Additionally, we offer a method to compute the minimal equations in $d$ and show that they have practical applications in finding irreducible polynomials over a finite field. Specifically, it can be used to answer a question posed by Glibichic and Tuza concerning irreducible polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_2$.

A novel Transient Voltage Protector (TVP) design relies on the rapid change in magnetization of a Symmetric Phase Angle Modulating (SPAN) transformer to safeguard against transient damage while ensuring no harm to connected equipment. This protection is achieved through two-core SPAN transformers where both cores are connected in parallel with the load in a specific configuration. As external magnetic fields exert a torque on the moving parts of the cores, and due to their initial position and alignment, they respond differently to these variations, resulting in a significant differential voltage between them during transient periods. This unique feature allows for the creation of a safeguarded SPAN TVP. For increased efficiency, a categorization system can be employed to divide SPAN TVPs into groups based on specific parameters such as their power rating, operating frequency, and differential voltage. This classification system can aid users in selecting the most suitable TVP for a given application.

In next-generation wireless networks based on millimeter wave technology, an improved quality of service for real-time applications can be achieved through multi-group broadcasting. To address this need, researchers are developing new encoding methods for multi-group broadcasting. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on separate group encoding, a novel hybrid encoding technique has been proposed, which combines elements of separate and common group encoding. By incorporating a hybrid encoding method, more efficient use of bandwidth can be achieved, supporting up to 8 simultaneous groups. As a result, better performance and higher quality of service for real-time applications can be achieved. Additionally, this hybrid encoding method allows for increased levels of hybridization, expanding its encoding capabilities and improving its performance. By incorporating an intelligent hybrid encoding method, network operators can achieve improved quality of service for real-time applications, even in challenging millimeter wave environments.

Let G be a group with an exponential residual finiteness property. This paper demonstrates that if G has a relatively small-dimensional characteristic subfactorial surface that contains no free products, then the dimension of this factor limits how rapidly G approaches residual finiteness. Specifically, for any group G with these constraints, the dimension of its characteristic subfactorial surface s scales as s^2 times the logarithm of the length of the group's generating set. This paper also proves that groups with relatively small-dimensional surface subfactoriality do not necessarily imply rapid residual finiteness.

This research examines the long-term behavior of a star-shaped graph network, consisting of multiple connected branches, where each arm is modeled as an Euler-Bernoulli beam. Considering the system's energy and rigidity preservation, we investigate the asymptotic stability of the resulting system and develop a Lyapunov-type system to describe its behavior over time. By demonstrating the system's energy and rigidity decay, we show that this model is globally asymptotically stable, provided that all arms of the star-shaped graph have identical properties. Furthermore, we extend this analysis to a network of coupled Euler-Bernoulli beams, where each arm is connected in a series and the system's energy and rigidity are also preserved. In this case, we show that the system exhibits a form of synchronization, where all arms of the network exhibit similar behavior over time.

Investigations into the nucleosynthesis of the r-process are heavily dependent on the machine learning model that utilizes experimental and theoretical data to create a global landscape of nuclear masses. This model, known as the WiML, is the foundation for future r-process studies, and it is critical that it achieves a high degree of accuracy given the narrow isotopic pattern predicted by theoretical models. In order to enhance the accuracy of WiML, we are utilizing the least squares method to fine-tune two key components: the shell effect correction and the residual energy correction. We are also exploring the feasibility of incorporating the linear momentum correction, a correction that is not currently utilized in WiML, into the model. To validate the effectiveness of these modifications, we are evaluating the predicted masses against the known masses within the r-process region and against the known masses across the entire chart of nuclei.

We have developed an extremely sensitive method for measuring the loss in sapphire, one of the purest materials available, with an accuracy of better than 10^-6 at high temperatures and better than 10^-4 at the dilution refrigerator temperature of approximately 20 millikelvin. Using an advanced technique that detects changes in dielectric loss, we found that anodized sapphire has extremely low loss, with an accuracy of better or equal to 10^-6, across a broad temperature range. Furthermore, we discovered that sapphire has negligible loss at the dilution refrigerator temperature, with an accuracy of better or equal to 10^-4 over a period of several minutes, which is crucial for the development of superconducting qubits.

The strength of an electric field that can be optically pulled towards a probe is determined by specific optical properties, such as refractive index and absorption, that are inherent to the medium and its structure. We demonstrate that this pull can be significantly amplified by modulating the light pulse in a particular manner and the medium's response accordingly. Notably, the required change in optical pull is achieved with minimal alteration to the refractive index, implying that the pull can be strengthened with minimal impact on the medium's bulk properties. We provide a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon, showing that it is rooted in the way the medium responds to modulated light at its resonance frequency. This discovery opens a new avenue for modifying light-matter interactions by manipulating pull-based forces at the nanoscale.

This paper develops a novel formulation for a class of robust optimization problems with binary constraints, characterized by uncertainties and requirements for reliability in critical systems. The framework is designed to minimize the worst-case scenario for performance measures such as cost, power, and energy, ensuring their satisfaction in critical situations. The problem is reformulated as a binary integer programming problem, but with a Lagrangian dual formulation that facilitates the use of efficient convex optimization algorithms. The Lagrangian dual approach yields a range of analytical solutions, including the optimal solution and upper bounds for the original problem. The method is effective in achieving tight bounds and accurate solutions, but the quality of the bounds depends on the level of variability, with performance degrading in systems with high levels of uncertainty. The approach is demonstrated to have good results for a variety of test cases, including a large-scale power planning problem with various levels of uncertainty.

The world faces numerous socioeconomic issues, prompting the need for research into diverse socioeconomic problems through the application of digital methods. A substantial challenge lies in accessing well-structured, comprehensive datasets that incorporate various modalities such as demographic, economic, transportation, and spatial information. To address this challenge, we have developed the H4M dataset, a comprehensive resource containing 20 million records from 2007 to 2020 across 1600 neighborhoods in Beijing. The dataset spans four categories: population, economy, transportation, and urban planning, incorporating different data formats including spatial, textual, and network data. Our analysis highlights the benefits of utilizing diverse datasets, particularly in mitigating issues related to data leakage and label noise. Furthermore, we demonstrate the value of incorporating diverse data sources by comparing the performance of machine learning models using data from the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Planning and Land, the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Statistics, and a combination of both sources.

We introduce a novel template-driven framework for data analysis, which enables
efficient processing of extensive datasets. Traditionally, statistical models
require extensive computational resources even for moderately large datasets.
In contrast, our approach leverages a visual template and is scalable to handle
enormous datasets. The templates define data structures and methods for
initialization and are written in a high-level programming language. The
metaprogramming technique used to implement the templates ensures real-time
execution without additional overhead. The templates can be utilized for a
variety of data analysis tasks, including visualization, filtering, and
classification. To accommodate custom requirements, user-defined methods can be
integrated into the templates. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated by
its ability to handle a dataset consisting of 10 million objects.

Deep Graph Neural Networks have gained popularity in handling graph data with node attributes, but their applications are often limited to specific domains due to model complexity and weight transfer issues. This study investigates graph neural architecture designs, particularly focusing on node classification tasks, to understand transfer learning. It reveals that current models predominantly consist of similar architecture components and that using similar components in transfer learning leads to similar model performance. To improve transfer learning, this study developed a method to automatically adjust architecture components based on the source model's performance, resulting in better performance on target datasets. The findings also suggest that models with better transfer performance share more similar neighbourhood structures, and that incorporating task-specific constraints can further enhance transfer learning.

Recommending relevant and appealing content to users is the primary goal of a suggestion system's (SS) designed to boost user engagement. The traditional approach to SS is limited to providing suggestions based on users' historical behavior, which is often inconsistent due to varying interests. To overcome this limitation, a new SS model incorporating dual feature distribution (DFD) is proposed. The suggested SS model is suitable for general content and can adapt to dynamic user interest shifts. The proposed approach is versatile and flexible, allowing it to be applied across different SS models. The performance of the proposed SS model was evaluated using Jaccard similarity and precision metrics on real-world Movielens-100k and Taggedmovielens datasets. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed SS model's enhanced performance and versatility.

We introduce an innovative, straightforward proof of the well-known Hypergraph Removal Lemma with exceptional applications to data streams, leveraging a newly introduced inverse conjecture known as the Minimum Bounded Linear Profile Number (MBL-PN). The MBL-PN has profound implications on linear profile bounds in various fields and can be utilized to derive the well-known Hypergraph Removal Lemma. The MBL-PN holds significant importance in its own right and is also applicable to data streams. The Hypergraph Removal Lemma has significant applications including a novel approach to solving the problem of set disjointness, which has substantial implications on data streams. The problem of set disjointness is a critical challenge in data streams, and our novel proof of the HRLE using the MBL-PN offers a fresh perspective on resolving this problem. The MBL-PN is a generalization of the Hypergraph Removal Lemma and has been used to derive the latter, and our new proof using the MBL-PN offers a fresh insight into this area of study. The MBL-PN is a generalization of the HRLE, and our new proof using the MBL-PN offers a fresh perspective on this area of study.
