The approach is simple to implement and efficient, making it a viable option for use in mobile apps and similar applications.

Chimeras are complex, two-part systems where connected oscillators behave differently, with one section often dominating the other. Chimeras exhibit distinct phases, with one area oscillating while the other remains in a state of equilibrium. This equilibrium may seem stable, but with a close examination it reveals a hidden, out-of-sync oscillation that seems to be ignored. This overlooked oscillation actually carries significant importance as it indicates when the equilibrium is actually stable or unstable. This neglected aspect will be the focus of this study, where we will show that when the out-of-sync oscillation is considered, chimeras display a level of stability that is evenly distributed across the spectrum.

Developing controllers that can handle unexpected events is a key challenge in creating robust controllers. Traditional methods for training controllers under uncertainty often assume a prior understanding of failure rates and system dynamics, which is rarely the case in practical applications. Our approach involves using a detailed model of a system's dynamics and any potential faults to guide a controller's training, effectively turning an uncertain design problem into an exploration problem where a controller's effectiveness is assessed under various scenarios. This initial work presents a general framework for policy exploration and provides a practical demonstration of its capabilities, including the development of a controller capable of handling partial data corruptions for a robot performing a task on a visual platform.

Multi-layer graphs are an extension of standard graph theory, allowing for the representation of relationships between different categories of objects. We introduce a combinatorial structure, the elevated slice algebra, as a multi-layer graph-based interpretation of a mathematical concept known as a slice. This algebraic object was first introduced by Ziegler in '06 as a multi-layer counterpart to the Boolean algebra. We demonstrate that elevated slice algebras can be represented as multi-layer graphs, with specific conditions on the graph's structure. We also define concepts of homomorphism and composition within elevated slice algebras, showing that they are equivalent to those in multi-layer graphs under certain conditions. This relationship allows us to identify key properties of elevated slice algebras by analyzing multi-layer graphs. We investigate the conditions necessary for the existence of elevated slice algebras in specific situations and provide examples of such algebras. We also establish a connection between the concept of cube algebras and the structure of elevated slice algebras.

We develop an approach to entropic phenomena in stochastic tensor networks by establishing a mirrored entropy correlation inequality. This inequality has a deeper connection to its quantum counterpart, with which it shares certain qualities and characteristics. By exploring this relationship, we uncover a locally equivalent operator orderings on commuting operator tensor networks, analogous to the Haag-Swerve function in conjugate pairing observed in Bell inequalities. This discovery is reminiscent of the connection between classical and quantum correlations as proposed by Shor's 1990 result. We demonstrate the relevance of our findings to the determination of the error rate in a specific noise model by comparing it to an existing stochastic tensor network scheme. We propose and evaluate an entanglement-based solution, as well as a classical algorithm, to the problem, and show that both methods yield the same result. We observe that both methods can be viewed as applications of a general approach to solving problems in the matrix-matrix product-dimensions class known as Zaslavskii tensors, with a time complexity of O(N^2) and a memory complexity of O(N, when N is the number of variables in the problem, as we show. We further show that our approach to solving the problem is robust to noise and can be generalized to solve a broader class of problems.

We analyze the patterns that emerge from interacting Markov processes, focusing on pattern evolution over multiple steps. Our findings indicate that persistent patterns with long-term significance are often tied to heritable data, which can be represented as conservative subsystems within the underlying Markov chain. By examining a wide range of examples, from simple models to more complex systems like the Jackknife model and Lotka-Volterra dynamics, we demonstrate that patterns with a lasting impact must, first and foremost, be heritable. This insight offers a powerful method for pattern analysis and sheds light on the inherent characteristics that enable patterns to endure.

The three-dimensional generalized Hénon diagram, defined by $x_{t+1}=\alpha x_t+\beta(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}+f(x_{t-1}))$, where $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$, is an iteration formula that lacks a clear fixed point and has complex dynamics. Despite this, previous studies have only explored one, two, three, and four-dimensional cases, leaving the three-dimensional case unexplored. Using numerical simulations, the dynamics of the three-dimensional generalized Hénon diagram have been analyzed through visualizations, mathematical derivations, and theoretical proofs. It has been shown that systems with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ values within a specific range can be stable, exhibiting periodic, semi-periodic, or chaotic behaviors. These systems can be divided into four distinct patterns, each corresponding to different attractor shapes. Theoretical proofs have confirmed the existence of these patterns, and numerical simulations have validated these findings, providing a foundation for future three-dimensional studies.

This research paper explores a theory of gravity that incorporates features of both Einstein and Weber, with the latter's theory viewed as a non-relativistic manifestation of general relativity.  By applying Weber's theory to a solitary entity, we demonstrate that the fundamental force of gravity can be expressed in terms of the Hesse matrix of a function, $f(u)$.  The paper then examines the properties of this function, $f(u)$, which we find subject to certain lower bounds and differentiability conditions.  By utilizing these conditions, we are able to derive the fundamental equation of gravitational force and its higher-order derivatives, which we then apply to the calculation of corresponding masses.  Furthermore, we are able to derive the expression for the gravitational force in terms of the first and second derivatives of a function, $f(u)$.  As a point of comparison, we have included a historical analysis of Weber's theory of gravity as well as a numerical evaluation of the gravitational force between two spherical masses, one of which is treated as a solitary entity.

For each $n\geq 1$, we calculate the distributions $H_2(n)$ and $H_3(n)$, which represent the total number of Young tableaux of specific hook length properties on the diagonal of the Young diagram of an orthogonal Young lattice points. Here, $H_2(n)$ counts tableaux where all hook lengths at diagonal points are even, and $H_3(n)$ counts tableaux where consecutive hook lengths at two consecutive diagonal points are either both divisible by 2 or both divisible by 3. These $H_2(n)$ and $H_3(n)$ counts are also related to the number of inversions in Young tableaux.

Using Larmor clock measurements, researchers have demonstrated the effect of spin oscillations on tunneling duration through the Larmor-Zee effect. The Larmor-Zee effect describes an alteration of the Larmor precession frequency in atoms with a non-zero electron spin, indicating the presence of a nearby particle's gravitational field. The study found that when two particles' spins oscillate in a synchronized manner, their tunneling duration is significantly reduced. The reduction in tunneling duration can be mathematically represented by an exponential expression. The experiment revealed that the phase difference between the two spins directly impacts the reduction in tunneling duration, observed to be on the order of 10^-16 seconds when the phase difference is π. The observed effects support the theories of tunneling and Larmor-Zee, and potentially open up new avenues for studying particle interactions.

We've derived the dominant distribution functions for P-wave mesons based on a novel, nonrelativistic effective theory. This theory incorporates a novel, dimension-4 operator not found in conventional QCD descriptions. Our results reveal that three distinct meson species - P-wave scalar, pseudoscalar, and vector mesons - all exhibit similar distribution functions. This finding explains why, in certain instances, P-wave scalar and pseudoscalar mesons appear to behave like Nambu-Goldstone bosons, even when they originate from a composite symmetry, despite not being true Nambu-Goldstone bosons. Additionally, we've determined the distribution functions for P-wave charm and bottom mesons, and we've also obtained the leading-twist distribution functions for P-wave baryons composed of one heavy quark and two light quarks.

A Bose-Einstein condensate provides an ideal setting for illustrating key principles of quantum mechanics, particularly linearity and superposition. When a system is described as undergoing multiple, distinct transitions is not accurately represented by linear equations. Quantum operators provide a way to mathematically translate a wave function into a measurable property. We show that linearity is a characteristic of quantum mechanics that can be seen as a consequence of how these operators behave. We use the context of a Bose-Einstein condensate, involving a single particle or two particles, to derive and examine the characteristics of these operators in relation to multi-state transitions. We also explore the relationship between these operators and their counterparts in classical mechanics. We find that operators corresponding to non-linear observables are defined by quadratic relationships with the Hamiltonian, and lie outside the scope of classical mechanics.

Recent research in soft gravities, including string theory and amplitudes beyond seven dimensions, has been reevaluated to find common ground with higher-spin field theories. By focusing on soft graviton operators within the BMS algebra, new definitions of double soft graviton principles have been established, building on previous work by Campiglia and Lusanna. The resulting theoretical framework leads to a novel formulation of soft gravity, characterized by two key properties: the absence of a conserved stress-energy tensor and the presence of vanishing central charge. The advantages of this approach include simplified stress-energy operators and the potential resolution of infrared divergences, notably the c-theorem. Theoretical applications of this framework are vast, potentially encompassing all areas of soft gravity, amplitudes, and the study of celestial holography.

The Neural Framework for Online Collective Continual Learning developed in this study is a first of its kind to tackle multiple learning tasks simultaneously, with each task being continuously updated as new data arrives over time. Unlike existing methods that use a fixed training approach, this framework enables real-time learning from a stream of incoming tasks and never stops acquiring new knowledge. Our framework excels at combining information across different tasks and maintaining a seamless flow of learning outcomes, even in the presence of noisy information and without access to task labels. Our approach relies on an innovative online meta-learning technique that continually adapts to changing data distributions and a collective online learning method that seamlessly integrates information from all tasks. Our results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our framework compared to state-of-the-art methods, both in an online setting and after training has completed.

In this study, the concepts of generalized shapes and measures are developed within the framework of Euclidean space. A particular case of these generalized measures is demonstrated to be equivalent to the recently introduced idea of shape measures. A specific instance of these generalized shapes and measures yields the concept of Ricci flat four-measures.

Permutation functions serve as a fundamental type of non-linear function in the realm of finite fields. A notable characteristic of permutation functions is that they have an inverse – in fact, the inverse of a permutation function is itself a permutation function. Research has shown that certain types of permutation function exhibit complete permutation behavior. A function $f$ from $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ to $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ is considered complete permutation if for every nonzero $x$ in $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$, the set $\{f(x)+\beta: \beta \in \mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}\}$ also contains a zero of $x$. In this study, we derive the general forms of permutation functions and complete permutation functions over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ and show that every permutation function $f$ from $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ to $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ has a unique $q$-Ricci matrix.

A major public health concern persists worldwide, characterized by intestinal
parasitic infections.  In order to effectively manage these issues, accurate
identification of intestinal worms in x-ray images is essential.  However, the
classification process is often hindered by low image quality and the presence
of noise, which can make manual categorization by experts difficult and time
consuming.  In this research, we present a novel method for automatically
categorizing intestinal parasites in x-ray images using Deep Belief Networks
(DBNs).  Our DBN model includes both unsupervised and supervised components
that can be combined in multiple ways, resulting in enhanced accuracy rates.  A
critical phase of our research was data preparation, where we applied image
enhancement techniques to improve DBN performance.  Our experiments involved
comparing the accuracy of four DBN models with different training processes
and various feature types, ultimately leading to the highest classification rate
of 94% for round worms.

In the reinsurance industry, non-zero-sum games between insurers and reinsurers have significant practical value in determining fair reinsurance rates and rewarding schemes. However, common mathematical models used in the industry often involve complex and difficult-to-solve partial differential equations. This paper presents an innovative approach to solving a type of non-zero-sum reinsurance game by utilizing two different models: the regime-switching Geometric Brownian motion model and the regime-switching jump-diffusion model. These models account for the uncertainty in the financial environment and the random nature of insurance losses. By applying the regime-switching models, which take into consideration the dynamic correlation between different market regimes, the partial differential equations involved can be simplified, making the estimation process more tractable and efficient. This paper also introduces a novel method for solving the reinsurance game under the regime-switching jump-diffusion model, which is more general and widely applicable than traditional models based on the Black and Merton models.

This research presents a new method for planning trajectories that incorporate dynamic constraints and variable wind currents. The challenge of navigating through turbulent air is an area often studied in the field of model aircraft simulation. Our approach involves breaking down the flight path into two stages: a preliminary assessment followed by a detailed refinement. The first step involves determining feasible flight routes with a predetermined speed, while the second step generates multiple possible trajectories near the target velocity to account for unpredictable wind conditions. Our method utilizes a genetic filter to ensure these trajectories meet specific control criteria, offering a high degree of stability and consistency in the results. Additionally, this planning process can be executed offline without consideration of real-time weather data, allowing for the generation of a pre-computed map of possible flight routes.

The fundamental low-energy interactions between pions and nucleons are a fundamental aspect of strong interactions, yet this sector remains theoretically underdeveloped due to a lack of data and challenging experimental conditions.  Chiral Effective Field Theory offers a framework to describe this complex interactions, but its applicability relies heavily on unknown high-energy interactions, which are modelled using unknown low-energy constants.  Our analysis reveals that low-energy pion-nucleon scattering can provide direct constraints on two specific low-energy constants and therefore provides a potential tool for determining high-energy behavior.  Furthermore, our findings suggest that future experimental efforts should focus on pion-nucleon scattering at energies below 300 MeV, as this would significantly advance our understanding of high-energy pion-nucleon interactions.

The CMS pixel endcap system's upgrade is part of the CMS tracker upgrade. For the upgrade, 24 blades on 50 modules in 8 planes will be used in each endcap ring. Due to the challenging environment of the forward region, the pixel blades were tested under intense conditions to ensure they can operate effectively. The pixel blades were designed to be long and thin, with a complex geometry that's difficult to model. As a result, the pixel blades were built in sections, and the sections were examined individually to establish a reliable understanding of their performance. The pixel endcap system utilizes a geometric reconstruction method to correct for any distortions in the strip and pixel geometry. The pixel blades were analyzed to verify that this correction method is accurate. The pixel blades were analyzed under various conditions to establish their performance capabilities.

A new machine learning framework has been developed to classify galaxy morphologies based on the shapes of their light. This method uses a two-stage approach with Gaussian Processes to simulate light profiles, training data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam survey and expert human annotators to generate accurate galaxy morphologies. Through testing and validation procedures, the accuracy of the trained framework reached 83% for bulge-disc separations and 77% for detailed morphology categorization. When applied to 10,000 active galaxies from the X-ray Bright Galaxy Sample, the framework provided reliable morphologies for 7,000 systems with high accuracy, enabling the identification of distinct galaxy types and sub-types such as early-type galaxies with discs. This method can be used to study the relationships between black holes and their surrounding galaxies at low to moderate redshifts.

Using ab initio methods, incorporating the effects of the strong short-range repulsion from quantum fluctuations has been shown to be crucial for understanding the properties of few-nucleon systems. However, the physics behind this short-range repulsion is still not fully understood, with some theories linking it to non-trivial features related to the baryon's self-energy, while others connect it to non-locality. In this study, a novel approach based on a quasiparticle effective action is presented to allocate the effects of short-range dynamics onto one-particle Green's functions. This formulation provides an intuitive understanding of the physics involved and allows us to derive a set of self-consistent equations for the quasiparticle wave functions and their properties. Utilizing this method, the effects of short-range dynamics on the distribution of nucleons and their momenta are analyzed, and the importance of including these effects, especially at high momentum, for the binding of the deuterium is demonstrated.

Recent breakthroughs in complex-valued deep learning have led to applications in fields like image processing and bioinformatics, with potential extensions to education. Researchers working in complex space have developed innovative methods, but have faced resistance from educators due to unfamiliarity. This resistance may stem from co-domain equivalence, the concept that classifier outputs must be confined to specific, limited value spaces to be universally accepted. The following discussion explores the implications of employing complex-valued deep learning in educational systems, with the possibility of expanding education boundaries through this approach.

We discuss the concept of geometric scaling as well as longitudinal and transverse momentum dependence saturation phenomena observed in QCD, using simple model representations. Geometric scaling is observed at a certain energy level in a broad range of $x$ and $Q^2$, but its occurrence depends on $x$ and $Q^2$ due to a phenomenon called a "GeV gap". This article also explores the connection between scaling behavior in $x$ and the momentum dependence of nuclear wave functions, particularly in high-momentum collisions of heavy ions. It uses a simple, non-linear model to demonstrate that geometric scaling in $x$ corresponds to a scaling behavior in rapidity distributions and that a similar non-linear process governs the acceleration of particles in rapidity and transverse momentum, mirroring the power-law growth of radial and energy density in non-linear elastic collisions of heavy ions.

The study of metal-poor, low-mass stars provides valuable insights into the earliest stages of star formation and the conditions that existed approximately 13 billion years ago. By examining a sample of 105 such stars in the Milky Way, researchers found that their distribution can be explained by two primary processes: (1) a uniform star formation event with a consistent efficiency across the sample's volume, and (2) a secondary mechanism where more massive, older stars release gas, which then forms new, younger stars. Statistical analysis revealed that the initial star formation event accounts for approximately 80% of the observed distribution, while the "gas-recycling" mechanism is responsible for around 20%. Furthermore, the study found that the average time between an old star's formation and its release of gas is around 1.5 billion years. The researchers note that this is consistent with the expectations for which stars will become gas donors, and that the star formation event is consistent with the expectations for uniformity on the scale of the sample's volume.

Theoretical machine learning forecasts are now widely applied in numerous fields, yet the evaluation of their performance remains underdeveloped. This study proposes a novel tool for assessing the sensitivity of machine learning forecasts, along with a practical demonstration of its use in literacy assessments based on adult reading tests. The suggested approach can be easily adapted for evaluating the performance of statistical models. The results indicate that the developed tool effectively identifies models requiring parameter adjustment. Furthermore, our study provides initial insights into the potential for machine learning models to predict literacy levels, laying the groundwork for future research in this area.

A new approach to quantum computing, based on a single Josephson Junction and Inverter system, is being explored. This platform could revolutionize the development of advanced quantum algorithms, potentially leading to their implementation on systems like SQUID and developing novel algorithms for machine learning and deep learning, as well as enhancing existing ones.

This study explores both local and global characteristics of warped product and
semi-incline submanifolds within nearly contact manifolds. Key findings include
theorems that establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the local
existence of such submanifolds, as well as criteria for their global presence.
Further, initial examples of globally existing warped product and semi-incline
submanifolds are provided, highlighting novel structures within the field.

The PALEOCCENE concept is a novel approach to detecting low energy nuclear recoils in a geologically shielded location. Utilizing a dark silicon carbide host with embedded vacancy-related color centers, it can identify recoiling nuclei at various speeds. The system boasts the distinction of being one of the few that can be easily moved to a site with minimal cosmic ray flux, further enabling the study of dark matter at exceptionally low recoil energies. Our current understanding of the technology is documented, along with projected count rates under Earth and cosmic conditions.

Colloidal particles move in response to fluid flow and interact with surfaces and other particles to form self-organized patterns. These patterns can attract or repel the particles due to their structural features, such as patterns created by fixed particles that trap flowing fluid. This study examines the movement of colloidal particles within a fluid flow to understand their interaction with evolving patterns of fixed particles and the resulting complex patterns that form a connection between the particle structure and the fluid's behavior.

This paper delves into the theoretical understanding of numerical observations that a broad range of charge densities support the magnetoroton eigenstate, a feature that might be experimentally quantifiable in the near future, opening doors for novel research. By employing perturbation theory, we analyze how a strong magnetic field influences the regulatory effect on the spectral total density, demonstrating that this effect can be finely adjusted. Moreover, we explore the feasibility of identifying chiral ghost edges through regulatory effects, thus paving the way for comprehensive studies of unconventional edge configurations.

We introduce a novel approach to detecting potential disease outbreaks on contact networks using real-world demographic data. A non-parametric statistical method is employed to identify unknown latent factors driving disease transmission, which often reflect social clusters. Notably, this approach can detect clusters without requiring prior knowledge of their existence or specific boundaries, making it a valuable tool for researchers. To achieve this, we leverage a silent network observer, allowing the researcher to view the disease spread dynamics without influencing it. A simulated study demonstrates the method's efficacy, which yields comparable results to established techniques such as Bayesian clustering. Furthermore, we apply this method to two actual disease outbreak datasets, highlighting its ability to uncover hidden social structures.

Researchers have proposed an innovative method for detecting foreground residues in CMB map restoration by utilizing the maximum probability principle. A key component of this approach involves setting the Gaussian map in question to zero inside and outside the foreground mask, effectively converting the problem into finding the best CMB estimate within the mask. However, the method's reliability heavily depends on the foreground map accuracy, particularly at the edges of the mask where algorithms can introduce artifacts. These artifacts manifest as "X's" around point sources of noise and appear in the residuals, which can be seen in the example of a noise source superimposed on a real foreground map in the analysis. To overcome this limitation, the researchers suggest combining the maximum probability principle with an additional step of subtracting foreground models of point sources before performing the restoration step, as demonstrated with an example using the AMI Galaxies map.

Our research focuses on resolving referential ambiguity in goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, where communication methods indicate goals rather than observed environments. Current natural language-based methods fall short because they often use natural language to communicate goals, introducing referential uncertainty. To overcome this challenge, we propose using artificial neural messages, separating the agent's representation of the environment from its goal representation. By doing so, we enable the agent to learn effective message representations and enhance its problem-solving abilities on complex tasks. Our proposed approach yields significant performance gains in existing referential communication tasks and allows the agent to learn efficient message representations that surpass state-of-the-art results. Additionally, we demonstrate that artificial neural messages facilitate generalization to novel environments and tasks, and our method can also be applied to more intricate tasks involving multiple goals, hierarchical objectives, and hidden goal parameters.

Quantum channel shadow tomography offers an efficient approach to state and operator characterization by utilizing pre-selected and measuremnt-induced states. Due to its cost-effectiveness, this method is well-suited for characterizing quantum channels within functional analysis frameworks. Notably, recent research has demonstrated the possibility of characterizing an arbitrary qubit channel using relatively few measurements, specifically 22 different quantum states. Building upon this concept, we propose an approach to accurately determine any qubit channel using an average of 22 different quantum states, with a lower bound of 14 states in certain scenarios. Additionally, we extend our method to characterize quantum channels within the realms of quantum finite-dimensional physics and free quantum systems.

In this research, we explore inequalities of the Keen type in relation to a standard shape, \epsilon-Riemann sphere, within two and three-dimensional spaces, specifically focusing on planar convex shapes in two dimensions. Previous findings by M. Keen were extended to three dimensions by J. McCleary and M. Keen, with later contributions from J. Zoppe. Here, we derive new inequalities for a specific standard shape in three dimensions, and prove a conjecture previously put forth by J. Zoppe.

This research delves into optimizing the path for micro-electromechanical devices, specifically a certain type of MEMS, to follow while above the ground, which requires them to maintain a certain altitude. The potential applications for these devices involve taking images or videos from an aerial perspective, and we've developed an algorithm to find the most suitable flight path for them to take images at specific times and maintain a certain altitude, while also minimizing the total time it takes for them to cover all assigned tasks. The algorithm we've developed uses a type of mathematical programming to solve the problem, and through simulations, we've demonstrated that this type of path allows us to solve the problem in a timely manner.

In our previous study, we employed a renormalization group method to analyze the structural and dynamical changes in low-energy Coulomb-interacting bilayer graphene, with a specific focus on its dynamics within the wavy phonon framework. This previous analysis revealed that low-energy Coulomb interactions in bilayer graphene give rise to an expansion of its wavevector space. Building on this previous work, the current study delves deeper into the impact of Coulomb interactions on bilayer graphene's dynamics by investigating multilayer graphene. We specifically found that for $N\geq3$, an expansion of the wavevector space occurs in a similar manner, with the Coulomb interactions in bilayer and higher-layer graphs exhibiting a notable similarity in their renormalization group equations. This correspondence allows for a straightforward extrapolation of our results to any $N\geq3$-layer graph, with the known structure of these equations suggesting that they may have multiple fixed points. We further hypothesize that these RG equations may have a critical point at $N\approx5$, with the presence of multiple instabilities in this region.

The conformation of doped fullerene (Sc2TbN @ C80) on a nickel oxide layer (h-BN/Ni(111)) changes with temperature. At high temperatures (600 K), the conformation is flat and two-dimensional, but drops to (5, 4) ring configurations on the nickel oxide layer when cooled to (300 K). To study this transformation, density functional theory (DFT) is used, where (6, 6)) ring configurations in Sc2TbN @ C80 are found to be energetically stable on the nickel oxide layer. Additionally, the theory shows that (Sc2TbN @ C80) adsorbed on the nickel oxide layer is more stable than (Sc2 @ C80) and (Tb @ C80) separately. The research also shows that (Sc2TbN @ C80) on the nickel oxide layer exhibits strong magnetic properties due to (Sc2) and (Tb) magnetic interaction, but (Sc2 @ C80) and (Tb @ C80) separately exhibit very low magnetic properties on the nickel oxide layer at (300 K).

The internet of things encompasses a diverse array of devices, including energy-efficient gadgets like sensors and actuators that operate on low power consumption, equivalent to that of a standard radio transmitter. Since these devices adhere to energy constraints similar to a standard radio transmitter, they can utilize the principles of radio frequency or infrared-based lightweight cryptographic algorithms to ensure secure communication and data integrity. This study examines various lightweight cryptographic algorithms used for authentication and data security purposes on the IoT devices, including Lightweight Cryptography algorithms like SPN, Feistel, SHA-256, SHA-512, AES, DES, 3-DES, RSA, Elliptic Curve cryptography (ECC), Hash functions, Block ciphers, Stream ciphers, Public key technologies (PKI), Public key infrastructure (PKI), and Digital signatures. The analysis delves into the advantages and disadvantages of these algorithms, as well as their practical applications, highlighting the need to strike a balance between security and energy efficiency in designs for the IoT.

The Ramsey series serves as a widely used method for measuring the persistent field in optically trapped ion experiments, including those involving ion traps and dipolar traps. This method involves alternating sequences of pulsed magnetic flux, with ions making Larmor spin precession measurements between each pulse. Key ion trap applications rely on accurate persistent field measurements, which presents a challenge due to the Ramsey estimate's sensitivity to noise and the inherent limitations of pulsed measurements. To address this issue, a novel approach has been developed that utilizes a sequential Bayesian method to design adaptive measurement sequences, minimizing the uncertainty in pulsed measurement results within a specified time frame. This approach can also determine the optimal sequence duration for a desired level of accuracy.

A new measure of network centrality, known as Gromov importance, is proposed, which is calculated by summing the surplus triangle inequalities for all nodes in the network. This approach recognizes the importance of shortest paths and their associated triangle inequalities, particularly through the lens of Gromov-hyperbolicity. By applying a multi-faceted centrality model to a network graph, a system of hierarchical importance is established, mapping key properties of shortest paths to a network's nodes. To demonstrate its effectiveness, Gromov importance is used to assess the centrality of nodes in genuine Gromov-hyperbolic networks, as well as in some non-hyperbolic cases. Furthermore, a visualization technique based on Gromov importance is described, which successfully highlights the characteristics of a network graph in accordance with its calculated importance values.

The Azimuthally Uniform Theory of Gravity offers an alternative to classical gravity, with its fundamental equation based on tensor calculus and a new insight into Newton's law of universal gravitation. This insight reveals that gravity behaves uniformly in a roundabout path, like an object placed on a turntable. Consequently, the theory's mathematical underpinning resembles Navier-Stokes equations, with gravity exhibiting analogous properties to fluid friction. With these grounds, the theory enables derivation of Poisson's equation for two masses of gravity as a consequence of the equation for one mass, much like Laplace's equation for two points as a consequence of the equation for one point.

We examine sets of matrix pencils, defining them as collections of matrix pencils that share the same Kronecker canonical form. Similarly, we look at sets of matrix pencils, defined as groups of matrix pencils in vector space equivalence. We are particularly interested in these two forms of equivalence when looking at the linearity of the resulting sets. Notably, we show that a set of matrix pencils is linear if and only if it can be brought into the same form through row and column operations. Additionally, we are exploring similar concepts for solving polynomial equations, inspired by a recent challenge in coding theory.

We have developed a geometric T-duality framework for twisted tori, which extends to n-dimensional tori with Hermitian flat connections. This framework provides a geometric understanding of T-duality for tori with non-trivial vector bundles, encompassing tori with symplectic, Kaluza-Klein, and Born-Infeld geometries. It involves combining the geometric T-duality transformation with a connection flatness requirement, and our work has led to new geometric solutions. Geometric T-duality has been demonstrated for one-dimensional and n-dimensional tori, and we have shown that it is a local symplectic transformation. Furthermore, we have found that it preserves the torus with a Hermitian vector bundle, and our work has been supported by examples.

In 2019, a theory called Parameterized Algorithmic Landscape was introduced by Weller and Zanotti Gallagher, which combines parameterized time complexity theory with parameterized depth-first search. As part of this framework, parameterized query theory was proposed, which involves studying query families that change depending on a parameter. A notable result in this field was discovered by Weller and Zanotti Gallagher, which showed that planar graphs have a certain type of query family reduceable to treewidth-based queries. This led to several subsequent findings, including a connection between parameterized query theory and the creation of parameterized algorithmic landscape, as well as a new approach to define parameterized depth-first search. As a continuation of this research, the current paper makes three significant contributions: it shows that k-apex minor-free and outerplanar graphs have a certain type of query family reduceable to treewidth-based queries, it proves that k-outerplanar graphs have a query family reduceable to pathwidth-based queries, and it shows that k-planar graphs have a query family reduceable to treewidth-based queries, all while changing with the parameter k.

For piecewise constant continuous functions, which exhibit monotonic behavior on separate intervals, we analyze a discrete system defined by its iteration formula. This formula maps atomic values to atomic values, where convergence properties are determined by the dynamics in local contraction centers. These centers, however, may not always exist under a general, widely applicable transformation, but such an existence is established under a specific condition in $\omega$-contracting systems, which also allows us to study stability in conjunction with the contraction expansion technique. These findings are illustrated by examples.

A new quantum algorithm called the Qubit-excitation-driven Adaptive Variational Quantum Eigensolver (qAVQE) has been created to find the lowest energy state of molecules within a given radius using a superconducting circuit. This algorithm starts by running a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) using a initial random variational circuit, then uses measurements of a specific excitation operator to determine the next variational circuit and iteratively improve the energy calculation. Unlike traditional VQE, qAVQE doesn't need a pre-determined sequence of circuits, making it more reliable. Results from simulations and real-world experiments show qAVQE's ability to find accurate energy levels and wave functions, even when using fewer qubits and fewer repetitions than necessary, and in cases when the initial variational circuit is random.

Deep neural networks function as complex, layer-wise transformers of data, and their reverse, the profound generative decoder, is a network that effectively reconstructs input data given a code, thereby enabling an array of applications including image and video compression, cryptography, and denoising. Notably, representations within the profound generative decoder are optimized to yield the highest likelihood mappings between the decoder's input and the underlying data distribution, a property unique to self-organizing maps. In this study, a technique is presented to extract meaningful representations from the profound generative decoder by approximating the maximum likelihood mappings using a mean-field approximation. A simple, yet efficient method is also proposed to refine these representations through iterative adjustments. When applied to code representations, these techniques exhibit notable improvements in the quality of the reconstructed input, and, importantly, the extracted representations far surpass those currently in use, demonstrating a superior capacity for dimensionality reduction and visualization. A source code implementation is available at https://github.com/philipn-p/representation-extraction.

Recent findings from NANOGrav's array of pulsar timing data suggest strong evidence for the presence of gravitational waves at a level that exceeds the expectations set by the Universe's large-scale structure and its evolution. This potential detection is crucial for defining the characteristics of stochastic gravitational waves, including their frequency and amplitude. A frequency-proportional amplitude has been consistently indicated by NANOGrav's data across various timeframes, and this trend is further reinforced when combined with Hubble's constant constraints. A frequency-proportional amplitude is also consistent with a rigidly amplified gravitational wave background generated by inflation, and this is reflected in a best-fit model that matches NANOGrav's data. However, this model's predictions are found to be inconsistent with the expected gravitational wave background generated by the Universe's large-scale structure and its evolution. A robust cosmological model that incorporates the Hubble constant and NANOGrav data has been developed and refined, and this model's parameters are found to strongly favor a rigidly amplified gravitational wave background generated by inflation. This is characterized by specific frequencies and amplitudes, and this model's validation is supported by the presence of residual frequency-dependent noise in NANOGrav's data that is yet to be fully accounted for.

We present observations of CS in the interstellar medium at an unusually high frequency of 110.7 GHz, specifically targeting the molecular cloud CAZ102 that contains the dark cloud CB230. This cloud is notable as it contains the comet-forming region of C/2015 ER61. Our analysis of CS emission reveals a centered peak with a line intensity of 13.1 sigma, observed using wideband linear polarized continuum and sideband separation techniques. Our analysis of CS emission indicates a Gaussian distribution with a 1 sigma width of 1.5 parsecs, aligned with the cloud's magnetic field. Our analysis of J=5-4 emission indicates a peak opacity of 0.5, suggesting that CS emission is optically thin. Our analysis of CS emission indicates a peak column density of 1.3*10^16 cm^-2, observed using a 30 km/s/tan beta method. Our analysis of CS emission indicates a peak abundance of 1.1*10^-9, observed using a 30 km/s/tan beta method. Our analysis of CS emission indicates a peak gas temperature of 17 Kelvin, observed using a 30 km/s/tan beta method. Our analysis of CS emission indicates a peak kinetic temperature of 25 Kelvin, observed using a 30 km/s/tan beta method. Our analysis of CS emission indicates a peak thermal velocity of 2.1 km/s, observed using a 30 km/s/tan beta method

We investigate the use of an underutilized technique for generating speech without training from pre-existing audio data. By employing underutilized data like written descriptions, filters can be learned to produce audible, coherent sounds. Past implementations of this method, however, required complex neural networks and were limited by their need for extensive training data. Our research builds on a previous approach with a simplified and more efficient solution. Our results demonstrate that this improved method can successfully identify and create distinct sounds within speech, utilizing simplified models and much less training data.

We examine the influence of a quintessence field with a complex phase on the holographic dark energy behavior, where the energy density of this field is used as an external adjustment to fine-tune the holographic dark energy parameters. Considering the Tsallis modification in the black hole geometry of a quintessence-dominated universe, we derive and analyze the holographic dark energy behavior in a static universe filled with cold matter. A complete thermodynamic system is constructed for this scenario, and key properties are identified: the relationship between pressure and energy density presents a phase transition behavior; a causality condition is satisfied; a null energy condition holds; and a thermodynamic stability condition is satisfied.

A multi-objective optimization problem, characterized by a substantial number of local optima and non-convex regions where gradient information is unavailable, poses a difficult solution-finding task even with computationally efficient simulations. Conventional multi-objective optimization methods, including evolutionary algorithms and heuristic techniques, have been found wanting in addressing these issues effectively. In response, a novel hybrid approach is proposed, which integrates a branch-and-bound technique with a non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm, specifically non-dominated simulation series (NSS). NSS is a multi-objective evolution strategy that enhances efficiency by leveraging previously computed results to expedite convergence towards optimal solutions, thereby reducing the need for costly simulations. When applied to the considered problem, this hybrid approach yields a notable improvement in performance, with solutions obtained through fewer evaluations being of higher quality. Furthermore, this technique enables the identification of promising regions within non-dominated frontiers, where further exploration using local improvement methods is recommended.

We explore the concept of linked Lie groupoids and their fundamental characteristics. A key finding reveals that any linked Lie groupoid can be seamlessly integrated into a stack on the underlying classical category, and this construction holds significant relevance in Synthetic Differential Geometry. Notably, linked Lie groupoids naturally arise as solutions to classical differential equations and play a crucial role in the study of smooth spaces. Building on these concepts, we establish that linked Lie groupoids possess inherent connectedness and wholeness when mapped into a stack. Moreover, our research demonstrates that the map from a classical Lie group to its corresponding dual groupoid involves an essential restriction, and this implication has profound implications for the study of invariant connections and, more broadly, for G-structures.

In the medical field, data from various sources including genomic sequencing, clinical trials, and imaging scans, are typically isolated and inaccessible due to differences in data format, which hinder comparative analysis and application. To overcome this challenge, we suggest utilizing a universal data access framework that enables secure data sharing and standardized processing, thereby allowing researchers to safeguard their data and ensure secure, efficient data transfer to and from local systems. By developing this framework, researchers can easily contribute to and utilize collective knowledge without compromising local data security and maintain control over their data. We will demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through real-world examples of biomedical data sharing.

Aspect-based emotion prediction is a critical sub-task in emotion analysis. 
This research paper investigates how to unlock the 'hidden sentiment' in NLP models 
for predicting specific emotions related to particular aspects of a given text.
These models, typically trained on general sentiment data, may struggle 
to identify the emotional nuances surrounding specific topics due to overfitting 
or generalization issues. To address this challenge, we propose a novel self-contrast 
method to refine a language model's emotional understanding without relying on 
emotion-annotated data. Instead, we utilize manually assigned sentiment labels 
to extract and categorize emotional sentiments, separating the original text 
from its associated aspects. This guided pre-training enables the model to grasp 
the emotional concepts surrounding specific topics more effectively. Experimental 
results on six public datasets demonstrate our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art 
methods in most cases, with particular improvements in detecting emotions 
related to well-known topics like 'iPhone' and 'Tesla'.

In medical studies, researchers use a special approach to case-control sampling when exploring the causes of a disease. It's essential to analyze how risk factors affect the disease through other potential influences, using data from existing studies. A binary mediator variable is also considered, affecting both the risk factor and outcome variables. We aim to evaluate the effect of a risk factor on the disease through the mediator, utilizing case-control studies. A statistical test has been developed to determine if the effect of the risk factor on the disease through the mediator is significant. A simulation study was conducted to assess the performance of the test under different study conditions. Real-world data from two medical studies, involving smokers and lung cancer patients, have also been used to illustrate the application of the test in practical scenarios.

This research paper delves into the secure communication network for multiple users assisted by a reconfigurable intelligent surface, with the network subject to performance constraints due to physical impairments affecting the signal strength. To maximize long-term and short-term security for all users, an optimization problem is formulated to enhance the QoS requirements through a two-stage approach. Firstly, the base station transmits data with optimal levels of secrecy interference using a pre-coder designed for imperfect feedback, while the reconfigurable surface reconfigures its elements to amplify desired signals and reduce interference using channel estimation. To address the lack of absolute accuracy in equipment limitations, an iterative algorithm is proposed to find a stable point for the reconfigurable surface elements, via a new method that utilizes duality and cuts down on feedback dependence. Simulation results confirm that our approach can achieve secure communication for multiple users with improved QoS, while demonstrating the impact of physical constraints on system performance.

To effectively implement a value-based approach to decision-making, we must first define the concept of state-value functions, which can be challenging in complex situations. We propose a strategy to overcome this difficulty by leveraging the benefits of re-sampling and re-naming techniques to facilitate learning and understanding. Our method involves re-defining state-value functions to better suit specific problems through re-naming, while also utilizing re-sampling to explore alternative perspectives and identify valuable insights. By applying these techniques, we can clarify the initial definition of state-value functions and ensure consistency. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through its application in the execution of re-sampling and re-naming, which can also be utilized in other areas of decision-making.

The solar wind's behavior near the Sun remains a significant mystery due to astronauts' inability to observe it. As a result, researchers rely on spacecraft that dare to venture close to the Sun, like the Parker Solar Probe, to uncover the underlying processes. By analyzing data from the probe's first encounter with the Sun, researchers found patterns in the solar wind's speed, density, and temperature that repeated over approximately 90 days. These observations suggest that the solar wind near the Sun is driven by the release of magnetic energy from the solar wind itself, which varies based on the solar wind's speed and density. This, in turn, influences the energy flow towards the solar wind, creating an intricate feedback loop. These findings provide new insights into the solar wind's behavior near the Sun and can be applied to develop more accurate models of the solar wind's behavior throughout the heliosphere.

The concept of noncommutative principal countable bundles is introduced as a direct extension of their commutative counterparts, found in [20]. These noncommutative bundles are defined as being locally isomorphic to the action of a discrete group within a C*-algebra, followed by the quotient map. Building upon this definition, it is demonstrated that a C*-algebra can be viewed as a principal countable bundle if and only if it can be locally isomorphic to the action of a discrete group within another C*-algebra, followed by the quotient map. Moreover, it is shown that a C*-algebra is expressible as the inductive limit of separable, unital C*-algebras if and only if it can be re-expressed as the quotient map resulting from a discrete group's action on another separable, unital C*-algebra.

In this paper, we explore the relationship between free ultrafilter chains, compact spaces and almost disjoint sets. We begin by providing a space characterization for the free ultrafilter chain property. This characterization is then used to demonstrate that every compact space with a certain uniform continuity property cannot be expressed as the union of an infinite, nested sequence of compact sets. This solution to a problem posed by van Mill can be derived from a theorem concerning the free ultrafilter chain property. The theorem is also applied to establish the non-existence of a compact, countable first-countable space satisfying the countable compactness property. A new concept, called the nearly disjointness value, is then introduced. This is analogous to the ultrafilter and compactness properties previously discussed. The nearly disjointness value is a compactness-like property that can be expressed as an inequality involving the cardinality of the space. The ultrafilter and nearly disjointness values are equivalent properties, and a compact space has the ultrafilter value if and only if it has the free ultrafilter chain property. The space X has the ultrafilter value if and only if every infinite, bounded subset of X has cardinality c. The almost disjoint set system P on ω can be expressed as the space X(ω) if and only if X has the ultrafilter value. The nearly disjointness value is a compactness-like property that can be expressed as an inequality involving the cardinality of the space. The ultrafilter and nearly disjointness values are equivalent properties

We've investigated the influence of $q$-deformation on optomechanical systems with intrinsic loss. Unlike conventional systems, which experience loss independently of mechanical motion, $q$-deformed systems exhibit cavity decay linked to mechanical motion. This work shows that $q$-deformation can enhance optomechanical transparency and coupling strength, particularly in single-photon and two-photon transitions. Notably, introducing $q$-deformation yields a robust and stable optomechanical crystal with improved properties, surpassing its non-deformed counterpart. This study also explores the potential for $q$-deformation to improve optomechanical performance even in the presence of mechanical dissipation.

We analyze the intrinsic wave functions of a novel type of R-parity violating supermultiplets, referred to as 'Double-Rotors', within the context of the Extended Quark Cluster Model. Each Double-Rotors configuration is characterized by two R-parity violating terms, resulting in a total of six possible states, as opposed to the usual eight, which are divided between even and odd parity states. Our investigation focuses on the 'adverse' R-parity violating modes, where the upper limits of the supermultiplet have positive R-parity, as opposed to the null modes, and as such, they are inaccessible to study via experiments. Using the group-theoretic method, we calculate the reduced transition matrix elements of the R-parity violating operators to the scissors modes, and find that the adverse scissors modes exhibit significantly higher transition strength to the ground state compared to their even parity counterparts. This property could potentially allow for the detection and identification of these modes.

A novel numerical approach, the cell-mean based neural network method, has been introduced for solving partial differential equations with high computational efficiency. This method can handle both hyperbolic and elliptic PDE systems, as well as their combination, within a fixed time-step framework. It's based on a cell-mean interpretation of the neural network, where the method can be viewed as an extension of the cell-centered finite difference method. Analytical error estimates and numerical case studies are provided to support the proposed method's convergence.

The ALICE detector at the LHC is being upgraded to take advantage of the LHC's highest energy collisions during Run 3. This upgrade will allow the ALICE to operate at an increased rate of 25 nucleon-nucleon collisions per second, up from 1.5 in Run 2. To take full advantage of the LHC's capabilities, the ALICE will run for as long as 50 inverse nanobarns during Run 3, resulting in a significant increase in the total luminosity from 20% to 100% of Run 2's levels. This report will outline the upgraded ALICE detector and the strategies being used to increase its performance in Run 3.

We investigate the temporal version of the Unruh effect and its connection to entanglement between past and future light cones, which can be observed by a free scalar field. Our analysis shows that the entanglement of light cones generates a geometric phase, analogous to the Berry phase, which arises due to the temporal translation and conforms to the Jaynes-Cummings model. To gauge the temporal Unruh effect, we propose an entanglement-based measurement method.

Our dataset includes 5,000 multi-sentence texts in eight languages, each representing a specific event in a person's life, such as getting married or graduating. This information is based on publicly accessible online biographies, thereby offering opportunities to enhance and correct existing knowledge. Our goal is to facilitate research into multilingual knowledge graph construction and knowledge base completion in multiple languages. The dataset is available at https://github.com/thesushil/multilingual-kb-construction.

The global structure theorem for characteristic forms of characteristic zero on a global vector bundle has been reinterpreted through the lens of a new formalism, which involves the use of push-forward equations. This push-forward formalism allows for the creation of a global subbundle with a specific geometric property, which in turn yields the original structure theorem. Additionally, this method has been extended to address other related questions.

The behavior of the wind from a star in close relationships with its companion significantly affects the X-ray emissions from the star, particularly in the way its density changes. Researchers used the NASA's NuSTAR space telescope to observe Cyg X-1, a black hole in the Milky Way, in its most intense phase and studied the effects of the wind from the star on January 2-3, 2015, during a period of enhanced mass flow. By analyzing the data, they discovered that the wind flow is at its highest during the times when the star's brightness also increases, suggesting a connection between the two phenomena. Moreover, they found that the density of the wind increases as it moves towards the innermost region, causing a decrease in the time it takes for the innermost circle to spin around the black hole. By modeling the changes in the density of the wind, they confirmed that the variations in the time it takes for the innermost circle to spin around the black hole are caused by the density of the wind. Finally, they proposed that the variations in the time it takes for the innermost circle to spin around the black hole can be used to determine the size of the region from which the density of the wind is measured.

A type of non-abelian gauge invariant operator inspired by aether theory is examined, characterized by its non-abelian nature and invariance to Lorentz transformations. It is found that this operator has no massless modes when the background gauge field is fully constrained. However, when the divergence of the background gauge field is not constrained, ghost-like modes emerge. At finite temperature, these modes become tachyonic when the background gauge field is non-zero. Furthermore, it is found that adding a non-abelian aether-similar term to the proton, a particle thought to be stable, results in stability under variations in proton composition. Utilizing the 't Hooft's Veneziano limit, it is confirmed that this term does not trigger chiral symmetry-threshold transitions.

The complex nature of text analysis necessitates a strong universal grammar, 
while also requiring flexible parsing to accommodate various semantic representations. 
In pursuit of this goal, we develop a collaborative text analysis framework, 
which leverages a network of universal grammar servers to generate a range of syntactic and semantic representations. 
To enhance efficiency and flexibility, we introduce innovative protocols for message passing between clients and servers. 
Furthermore, we establish a decentralized network registry to facilitate connections between untrusted clients and servers. 
Through our approach, the assembly line-like collaborative process is broken down into discrete, modifiable stages. 
We demonstrate the feasibility of this idea by implementing a collaborative text analysis system, 
which we evaluate using machine translation and abstract interpretation tasks. 
The results show that our approach can yield high-quality outputs, and modifications to individual servers have a direct impact on performance.

The primary source of energy powering short duration gamma-ray bursts with magnetically neutronized components is believed to be an accretion disk fueled by a neutron star or a black hole. Following a merger resulting in the formation of a black hole from a low-mass x-ray binary or a neutron star, the initial accretion phase is characterized by neutrino cooling and a strong magnetic field. As the neutron star evolves into a black hole, its surface temperature may decrease, but the disk may continue to feed the black hole with mass, causing it to spin faster. Using the general relativistic GRMAD code, researchers simulated a sequence of magnetized accretion disks with varying spin rates, from those of low-mass x-ray binaries to black holes with spin rates near the maximum possible value. They discovered that as the black hole's spin rate approaches its maximum value, the disk may transition from a traditional thin disk to a different type of disk called an advection-dominated disk, potentially slowing the black hole's spin rate in a manner that is consistent with observational data. This study provides a theoretical framework for understanding post-merger exits from accretion disks and suggests that black holes from low-mass x-ray binaries may have slower spin rates when they evolve into their final state.

The early-type galaxies in the distant universe hold crucial clues to understanding cosmic evolution. Specifically, the enlargement of early-type galaxies over time is thought to be influenced by the merger of smaller galaxies. To explore this, we analyzed data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam, which allowed us to identify an unusual class of early-type galaxies called ELGs that exhibit distinct red or blue color patterns in the early stages of the universe. By studying these ELGs, we discovered that they are characterized by a higher proportion of blue light in the early stages of the universe, which gradually shifts to red as they mature. Using advanced computer models, we found that this color pattern can be accurately replicated by simulating the merger of an average galaxy with a smaller, more compact galaxy. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that these mergers predominantly involve smaller galaxies and infrequently occur in galaxies with the same color pattern as the host ELGs. By analyzing the properties of these submerging galaxies, we found that they are typically less massive than their host ELGs and have a distinctively different structure. Lastly, our results indicate that these mergers are relatively rare events and are more likely to occur in galaxies with a certain mass range than in those with a more variable mass.

The Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravitation, developed in a previous study, has been further explored in relation to bipolar ejections, such as those observed in X-ray binaries and microquasars, revealing a repulsive force acting on ejected material and influenced by the presence of a surrounding accretion disk. This theory predicts that bipolar ejections occur at the center of the accretion disk and are directed either directly towards the center or in the opposite direction. As the ejected material travels, it experiences a force that repels it due to the curvature of space-time, causing it to accelerate and potentially reach speeds much faster than the accretion disk. This theory also provides an explanation for the variety of ejected masses and ejection speeds, suggesting that small ejection masses and speeds result from the presence of highly curved space-time and weak gravitational influence, while large ejection masses and speeds result from the application of this force over a longer period of time.

Researchers have observed a delayed radio burst in the vicinity of 2020hfx2, a known Fast Radio Burst source.  By analyzing the afterglow of 2020hfx2, as well as four other similar events, researchers found that these radio bursts typically emit less than 10^43 erg per second of optical radiation.  It is theorized that this radiation is a result of either a charge transfer process or due to the electrons in the magnetized wind of the source being accelerated.  If the former is true, then the emission from these bursts is likely to be significantly stronger than what has been observed so far.  If the latter is true, then the emission from these bursts is likely to be significantly weaker than what has been observed in certain cases, such as 2020hfx2.  By combining the data from these bursts with other data, researchers have placed new constraints on the emission from these bursts, as well as their precursor and post-cursor emissions.

To improve the high-power capabilities of laser systems, advanced techniques such as spatial filtering, 
high-average-power oscillators, and deep UV direct frequency tripling have been leveraged. The application of 
Bessel-Gauss optimization has also enhanced the beam quality and increased the output of laser systems. Furthermore, 
constructive techniques have been employed to rectify aberrations within these systems' resonators. These methods, 
coupled with numerical simulations, have facilitated the design and optimization of laser systems. The removal of 
aberrations and distortions has resulted in higher brightness and more efficient energy transfer in these systems. 
The integration of numerical simulations has facilitated the development of high-power laser systems, yielding numerous 
examples, including advanced oscillators, high-average-power amplifiers, frequency conversion, and beam shaping 
techniques.

To effectively combine text generation with visual control, we developed a task where language models produce descriptive text based on images and instructions. However, conventional approaches that rely on pre-existing image-text data for training are limited by the scarcity of image-text pairs, especially when instructions are involved. Our solution is a two-phase training method, starting with text generation without image inputs, followed by a text refinement stage that incorporates visual controls and image inputs. This unique strategy enables text generation models to operate in a world where objects and their visual counterparts exist independently. Our results on Frechet-Keithley Index scores demonstrate the superiority of this method over competing techniques.

Our proposed Delegated Ring Signature (DRS) scheme enables a designated group of verifiers to collectively sign transactions, thereby enabling a more efficient anonymous payment system. DRS subsumes both Boneh-Lynn-Shaw (BLS) ring signatures and their variants, as well as previous delegations of RingCT signatures. A detailed analysis of DRS's security and privacy has been conducted, building on first-of-their-kind results in these areas. In comparison with other anonymous payment systems, our scheme demonstrates superior performance and is more resistant to brute-force attacks due to lower total signature sizes and a reduced number of signatures required. A prototype implementation of DRS has been developed and is available for public use.

We propose a method called Brightness Scans to evaluate the beam quality of a laser system, such as an amplifier. The method involves using a 2D image sensor to detect the beam's spatial intensity distribution as it emerges from the amplifier. By manually rotating the sensor to cover all possible orientations of the beam, we can determine the diffusion of the beam's intensity distribution in the transverse plane. The degree of diffusion can serve as an indicator of the beam's coherence. We've demonstrated the method with an experimental evaluation of an Yb:YAG disk amplifier at the Max Born Institute.

In the context of collaborative learning, we explore modeling the dynamics of knowledge sharing between subjects.  By assuming each subject's knowledge to be a combination of their unique understanding and the understanding they have of other subjects, we develop a probabilistic framework that can distinguish between a subject's unique knowledge and their understanding of others.  This distinction enables us to identify and mitigate knowledge overlap and redundancy in modeling, ultimately leading to a greater understanding of each subject.  Our proposed method is generic and can be applied to a wide range of probabilistic models.  We evaluate its effectiveness using multiple state-of-the-art models on diverse datasets and find that it significantly enhances collaborative learning performance.

We investigate the decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into a $\Upsilon(nS)$ state
accompanied by $\pi^+\pi^-$ particles. Since the $\Upsilon(10753)$ cannot be produced
through a two-body decay of the $\Upsilon(10585)$ in current experimental technology, its
existence suggests the presence of an additional mechanism for its formation. A hadronic loop
process is proposed to explain the decay of $\Upsilon(10753)$ into a $\Upsilon(nS)$ state
along with $\pi^+\pi^-$ particles. This study aims to verify the proposed loop process and
relate it to the recently discovered $\Upsilon(10753)$.

We've developed a novel optimization method, specifically designed for quantized neural networks, to minimize the gap between quantized models and their full-precision counterparts. By incorporating range-constrained optimization, where we find the optimal solution within a limited parameter space, we've created AskewSGD. This method first gradually expands the search space in small, contiguous steps, systematically increasing the range and interval width until it reaches the full precision space. Along the way, we employ a technique called "askew" training to explore symmetric ranges, where we randomly shift parameters outside the current search space to maintain thorough exploration of the parameter space, promoting diverse solutions and robust generalization. We've successfully tested AskewSGD on various quantized networks and showed significant improvement over traditional methods, achieving up to a 0.9% reduction in top-1 accuracy gap on ImageNet when compared to the state-of-the-art Quantization-aware training approach. The code for AskewSGD can be found at https://github.com/ashishghodake/AskewSGD.

Over the past few decades, advancements in robotics have led to the development of robots as tools for medical treatment. However, robots struggling to navigate soft human tissues have hinderly limited their clinical impact. To fill this void, a new area of research, model-driven control of soft robots, aims to create robots capable of safely and effectively manipulating tissues. By employing computational models and sophisticated control techniques, these systems can adapt to changing soft robot interactions. Despite some recent successes, there are still numerous technical hurdles to overcome before model-driven control can be applied in life-critical medical procedures. This paper provides an in-depth review of the current state of model-driven control methods in soft robotics and identifies the pressing challenges that need to be addressed.
This short note rectifies a critical error in the authentication process of the Jacobi group as described in [arXiv:2103.1259], and provides a revised evaluation based on the correct results.

In the realm of Verifiable Machine Learning, the disintegration approach enables AI systems to validate structured fact sets by leveraging established knowledge graphs. Unlike general-purpose disintegration methods, AI systems face challenges when trying to disintegrate the base knowledge graph from given fact sets, prompting the development of tailored methods. Our study examines the feasibility of learning disintegration for fact set validation, particularly for scenarios where the base knowledge graph is large and cannot be modified. We introduce the Table2Graph problem, where we aim to generate a smaller graph subset that matches a given fact set, and propose two solutions. We evaluate these methods against a dataset composed of 1,918 table facts derived from the DBpedia dataset and show that they effectively reduce the size of fact sets while accurately representing the given facts in most cases.

This research introduces the Hidden Space Conditioning technique to improve
Generative Confrontational Networks (GCNs). The HSC method wraps an embedded
network within a larger framework, utilizing the embedded network's output
as conditioning information. This setup enables the main network to process
information from multiple sources, expanding the scope of conventional
autoencoders. In experiments with three datasets, we found that HSC networks
featuring a specific configuration of embedded and main networks (both using
ReLU-Elu activation) consistently demonstrated superior performance, with the
embedded network typically being a smaller version of the main network.
Notably, the combined parameters of these two networks often yielded a more
competitive result compared to using the total parameters for a single,
standalone network.

In a typical scenario involving audio in a room with multiple sources, sound waves exhibit periodic patterns due to the environment's geometry and scattered wave interference. To capture these patterns, a synchronized audio recorder is placed at a strategic location. We propose an audio analysis technique, called Hierarchical Sampling, that can accurately reconstruct the audio environment given limited data. For practical applications, a feasible recording setup might involve multiple, independently recording devices, each obtaining non-synchronized data. To address this, our algorithm can combine data from different recorders, leveraging patterns from each device to enhance the resulting audio. Although the audio environment's patterns can be discovered using an unwinding approach, we cannot guarantee that this discovery is the unique, original pattern. To resolve this, our method uses a new analysis technique, called Coarse Graining, that helps to reduce potential pattern misinterpretations by ensuring that the analyzed patterns are consistent over specific time intervals. To facilitate real-world applications, our algorithm has been adapted to work with a synchronized recorder consisting of multiple devices, each equipped with distinct characteristics, or phase samplers. For instance, to achieve high-quality audio, a high sampling rate is required, but this can be challenging to obtain in low-cost recorders. To overcome this limitation, our method allows the combination of data from different recorders, each operating at different sampling rates. We have tested our approach and found that it successfully reconstructs the audio environment, even when using non-synchronized, low-sampling-rate recorders and

In planar graphs, we've developed an efficient 'fault-resilient distance labeling' system, allowing any point to calculate its distance to any other point, even in cases where some points fail. This system requires just one bit of storage per point and offers a high level of fault tolerance, capable of withstanding a substantial number of point failures. Specifically, we've created a labeling system that uses storage efficiently, even in situations with a high number of point failures. This system works by dividing the planar graph into regions, ensuring that any point in a given region knows it has failed if at least k other points in that region have failed. We've found that, in planar graphs, it's possible to create these regions in such a way that the distance between any two points in the same region is always relatively close. This, in turn, enables us to develop a fault-resilient distance labeling system that offers a high level of fault tolerance and requires only a small amount of extra storage.

Our study examines correlations within a modified Bose-Hubbard model characterized by significant site-to-site interaction strength, varying levels of dissipation, and an externally imposed period of oscillation. By focusing on the links between these correlations in the system's behavior, we investigate the relationships between moment and spectrum analysis.
